question: How many daily medications do doctors usually mean when they talk about polypharmacy?

options.A: Taking two or more medications daily
options.B: Taking ten or more medications daily
options.C: Taking only herbal remedies alongside drugs
options.D: Taking five or more medications daily

explanation: You'll often hear this in the ward! Polypharmacy simply means a patient is taking five or more regular medications at the same time. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h1)

question: What is the main difference between good (appropriate) polypharmacy and bad (problematic) polypharmacy?

options.A: Problematic polypharmacy only occurs in hospital intensive care units.
options.B: Problematic polypharmacy means the patient refuses to swallow pills.
options.C: Appropriate polypharmacy has clear clinical benefits that outweigh risks.
options.D: Appropriate polypharmacy involves only traditional herbal mixtures.

explanation: Taking many drugs isn't always bad if every single pill has a clear job that helps the patient more than it harms them. That's appropriate polypharmacy! [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h1)

question: What do we call it when a drug's side effect is mistaken for a brand-new illness, leading to another prescription?

options.A: Treating a drug side effect as a new disease by adding another drug
options.B: Stopping all medications abruptly when a patient feels better
options.C: Switching a brand-name drug to a cheaper generic alternative
options.D: Taking a double dose of medicine because a previous dose was missed

explanation: This is a sneaky trap called a prescribing cascade! Instead of stopping the offending drug, a new drug is added to treat the side effect, making the pill burden worse. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h2)

question: How does fragmented healthcare (visiting different clinics without coordination) lead to polypharmacy?

options.A: Government policies limit the number of drugs a clinic can buy at once.
options.B: Different specialists prescribe drugs without knowing what other doctors ordered.
options.C: Patients intentionally hide their pill bottles from nurses during ward rounds.
options.D: Pharmacists refuse to dispense medicines prescribed by general practitioners.

explanation: When doctors don't talk to each other, a patient might end up getting duplicate or conflicting drugs from different specialists. Communication is key! [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h2)

question: What happens during a pharmacokinetic drug interaction?

options.A: One drug changes how the body absorbs, metabolizes, or excretes another drug.
options.B: The manufacturing company changes the active chemical ingredients.
options.C: Two drugs fight each other directly on the surface of the skin.
options.D: The patient develops an allergic skin rash from eating certain foods.

explanation: Think of pharmacokinetics as what the body does to the drug. If one drug messes with how the body handles another (like blocking liver breakdown), that's an interaction! [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h3)

question: Why are elderly patients much more sensitive to side effects when taking multiple drugs?

options.A: They refuse to take any form of liquid medication or syrup.
options.B: Their immune systems reject synthetic chemical compounds instantly.
options.C: They always forget to take their medications at the correct hour.
options.D: Their bodies process and clear drugs more slowly due to aging organs.

explanation: As organs age, the liver and kidneys don't clear drugs as fast. This causes medications to hang around longer and build up in the body. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h3)

question: What is the main goal of medication reconciliation?

options.A: To destroy any expired herbal remedies found inside the patient's home
options.B: To calculate the total financial cost of treatment for the hospital billing department
options.C: To create an accurate, complete list of all drugs a patient is taking across transitions of care
options.D: To force the patient to buy all their medications from the hospital pharmacy

explanation: Medication reconciliation is like making a master list. Whenever a patient moves from home to the ward (or ward to discharge), we check every single drug they are taking to prevent mistakes. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h4)

question: As a nurse doing medication reconciliation for a new patient admission, what is the best first step?

options.A: Copying the medication chart from the previous clinic without speaking to the patient
options.B: Asking the patient to bring in all current medication packages and herbal remedies from home
options.C: Waiting until the patient is discharged before checking their pill bottles
options.D: Prescribing a mild vitamin supplement to replace missing prescription drugs

explanation: Seeing the actual bottles, sachets, or herbal mixes prevents missing crucial details that patients might forget to mention verbally. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h4)

question: What does the term 'deprescribing' mean in clinical practice?

options.A: Writing a brand new prescription after a patient loses their drug chart
options.B: Increasing the dosage strength of a drug to make it work much faster
options.C: Switching a patient from tablets to intravenous injections in the ward
options.D: The planned, supervised process of stopping or reducing unnecessary medications

explanation: Deprescribing isn't abandoning a patient—it's a clever, safe way to trim down unnecessary pills and reduce side effects under medical guidance. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a good nursing strategy for helping a patient manage multiple medications?

options.A: Encouraging the use of weekly pillboxes or organizers to track daily doses
options.B: Educating the patient on recognizing early warning signs of adverse drug reactions
options.C: Collaborating with the pharmacist to simplify complicated dosing schedules
options.D: Telling the patient to stop all their medications immediately without consulting the doctor

explanation: Never tell a patient to drop all meds at once! Stopping drugs abruptly can cause dangerous withdrawal or rebound health issues. Changes must always be planned. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h5)
